public_text.4: C7 and C4 are right to focus on the h6+ line as the only forcing way to restrict Kg5. After 34...h6+ the king truly has two candidate squares, but Kf6 is the riskier choice because it steps onto the open e-file where Re8 can immediately coordinate with the knight for discovered pressure, and it also leaves the a5-queen with potential interposition ideas along the fifth rank or a-file once the knight moves. Kf4 keeps the king more contained toward the f/g complex, where the Rb2 already cuts the second rank and the knight can safely reach g4 without allowing any capture or block. That delivers mate cleanly by covering f2, f6, h2 and h6 while the pawn on g6 seals the remaining flights. Re6 after Kf6, as C6 suggests, loses a tempo because white can then interpose or capture on the e-file before the knight coordinates, turning a potential mate into a longer sequence.
